epics.title: Foundation, contracts, and reproducibility
epics.outcome: Explain the architecture, freeze a verified baseline, and start a buildable .NET/Aspire skeleton.
epics.exit_criteria: A fresh checkout restores, builds, and starts the skeleton; the API and synthetic data contracts are documented.

epics.title: Observable .NET support workflow
epics.outcome: Implement the Chapter 7 request path with working tools, routing, DevUI, and telemetry.
epics.exit_criteria: Demonstrate orders, billing, and technical requests and follow a request from HTTP entry through model/tool spans.

epics.title: Conversations, approvals, and streaming
epics.outcome: Preserve conversation state and safely pause/resume side-effecting work.
epics.exit_criteria: Demonstrate a follow-up, approval rejection, approved refund, restart/resume, cancellation, and streamed error.

epics.title: Safety, reliability, and measurement
epics.outcome: Enforce business boundaries and measure behavior and resource use.
epics.exit_criteria: Show unauthorized access rejection, bounded failure handling, and a baseline evaluation with honest cost/quality limits.

epics.title: Python implementation and behavioral parity
epics.outcome: Rebuild the complete behavior idiomatically in Python and compare SDK choices.
epics.exit_criteria: The shared evaluation runs against both backends with isolated state and comparable telemetry.

epics.title: One frontend for both implementations
epics.outcome: Add a browser experience over the shared backend contract.
epics.exit_criteria: Select a backend when starting a conversation, chat, approve/reject an operation, and diagnose a failure.

epics.title: Engineering evidence and interview readiness
epics.outcome: Demonstrate the system, defend decisions, and state its operational limits.
epics.exit_criteria: Complete a fault demonstration, publish a reproducible runbook, and answer a recorded or written mock interview.

tickets.title: Audit Chapter 7 and record a verified version baseline
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Recheck releases, runtime support, provider requirements, and prerelease dependencies.
Map the .NET and Python request paths and confirm the audit findings.
Write docs/decisions/0001-version-baseline.md with candidate versions, source links, and an explicit verification plan.
acceptance: The decision distinguishes observed versions from restore/build-tested versions.
Explain which security/refund path is actually hosted and identify one documentation/source disagreement.
learning_outcomes: Separate framework concepts from provider/hosting integrations.
Read migration notes and resolve stale course examples.
interview_questions: How do you establish that a tutorial is compatible with the SDK you selected?
Why can core be released while DevUI or hosting remains prerelease?
tickets.stretch: Find one additional assumption in the capstone and prove or disprove it from tagged source.

tickets.title: Define shared support contracts and synthetic fixtures
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Define schemas for requests, triage, responses, approvals, errors, and planned stream events under contracts/.
Seed synthetic customers, orders, policies, and an evaluation scenario format under fixtures/ and evaluations/.
Record ownership and state-isolation rules; preserve original user text beside derived routing fields.
acceptance: Examples include a valid request, missing order, unknown order, denied operation, and invalid route.
Schema checks reject invalid categories/ranges; fixtures contain no real personal data.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish schema validity, factual validity, and business authorization.
Design a language-neutral observable contract.
interview_questions: Why does structured output not guarantee a correct or authorized operation?
What should be shared between equivalent C# and Python implementations?
tickets.stretch: Add an ambiguous request and describe the expected clarification behavior.

tickets.title: Scaffold .NET support API and C# Aspire AppHost
tickets.source_note: The course composition roots are comparison points; Chapter 7 does not implement Aspire.
implementation: Create apphost/ and src/dotnet/ with the selected compatible SDK/package versions.
Add configuration validation and a health endpoint; keep support behavior unimplemented.
Launch the API through Aspire and document exact local prerequisites and startup commands.
acceptance: A clean checkout restores/builds and starts the API through AppHost.
Health is visible; missing provider configuration yields an actionable startup message without leaking a key.
learning_outcomes: Separate process orchestration from agent workflow orchestration.
Understand composition roots, configuration, and health.
interview_questions: What does Aspire manage, and what remains the application's responsibility?
Where should provider credentials and service endpoints be configured?
tickets.stretch: Change the local service port and prove the AppHost-provided endpoint still works.

tickets.title: Add reproducible builds and meaningful offline CI
tickets.source_note: The course dependency manifest motivates reproducibility; CI is an extension beyond the capstone.
implementation: Commit the runtime selector, central package versions, and dependency locks established by a successful restore.
Extend CI to build the AppHost/API and run meaningful contract/configuration tests using fakes.
Keep a stable always-reported required aggregate check and document offline versus live verification.
acceptance: A clean CI run needs no model credential and fails for a deliberate contract/configuration regression.
Branch protection requires the aggregate result; a skipped path does not create a permanently pending check.
learning_outcomes: Reproducibility and dependency locking.
Design CI around real failure modes and required-check behavior.
interview_questions: How do you test an agent application without paying for model calls on every PR?
Why can path-filtered required workflows block merges?
tickets.stretch: Reproduce a failed CI check locally from the documented command.

tickets.title: Build the first .NET order-status agent and DevUI
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Create one support agent with a typed order-status tool backed by synthetic fixtures.
Expose the same core behavior through the support API and development-only DevUI.
Provide deterministic tool tests plus a separately invoked live smoke check.
acceptance: Known and unknown orders produce factual outcomes and no invented status.
DevUI discovers the agent; tool execution is observable and the startup command is documented.
learning_outcomes: Understand the model/tool invocation loop.
Keep agent construction reusable across API and development tooling.
interview_questions: When should a model call a tool rather than answer from its prompt?
How does DevUI relate to your application API?
tickets.stretch: Remove the order ID and require a clarification without calling the lookup tool.

tickets.title: Export traces, metrics, and structured logs to Aspire
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Instrument the HTTP request, agent/model calls, and tools with correlated spans.
Configure explicit metric and log export and resource names/version.
Keep sensitive capture opt-in; add request/error counts and latency measurement.
acceptance: A success and a failure appear with correlated logs and useful span status.
Actual metric samples arrive in the dashboard; identify sources/meters and avoid counting one model call twice.
learning_outcomes: Separate instrumentation, providers, exporters, and the telemetry backend.
Distinguish traces, logs, counters, and distributions.
interview_questions: Why does seeing a trace not prove metrics are configured?
How do you correlate a request while avoiding sensitive data in telemetry?
tickets.stretch: Break the OTLP endpoint and explain the failure from application/exporter diagnostics.

tickets.title: Implement validated triage and deterministic routing
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Produce a typed triage decision with an allowed route and validated ranges.
Build explicit conditional routes and a fallback for invalid/ambiguous decisions.
Pass original request context and validated entities alongside the routing decision.
acceptance: Orders, billing, and technical fixtures take the expected route.
Malformed JSON, invalid category, and incomplete requests produce controlled fallback/clarification.
learning_outcomes: Use LLM classification inside deterministic control flow.
Understand generated confidence is not calibrated correctness.
interview_questions: What should be deterministic in an agent workflow?
How would you detect and improve poor routing?
tickets.stretch: Add an out-of-domain request without introducing another specialist.

tickets.title: Complete .NET billing and technical specialists
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Implement read-only billing and technical tools over fixture-backed services.
Give each specialist only its required tools and preserve source identifiers in answers.
Add scenario checks for invoice lookup, knowledge search, and ticket creation.
acceptance: All three domains work through the public support path.
Unknown records and failed searches are handled; a technical request cannot invoke a billing mutation.
learning_outcomes: Design scoped capabilities and factual tool-backed answers.
Understand single-agent versus specialist tradeoffs.
interview_questions: When do specialist agents justify additional model calls?
How do you prevent a specialist from exceeding its intended capabilities?
tickets.stretch: Compare one request with a single-agent baseline and record the call-count tradeoff.

tickets.title: Add per-conversation sessions and preserve context
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Map public conversation IDs to isolated agent/workflow state.
Support follow-ups using original user context and validated order/customer fields.
Define bounded history behavior and test concurrent conversations.
acceptance: An order follow-up works without repeating the ID.
Two conversations with different customers never see each other's history; model-generated summaries do not become authority.
learning_outcomes: Separate agent object lifetime from conversation state.
Understand history, session state, and context limits.
interview_questions: Can a reusable agent be shared while conversations remain isolated?
What belongs in conversation history versus application state?
tickets.stretch: Simulate simultaneous requests to one conversation and define the conflict policy.

tickets.title: Require bound approval for refunds and cancellations
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Wrap mutating tools in the current framework approval mechanism.
Expose pending action details and submit approval/rejection against the exact pending operation.
Enforce eligibility and customer access in the tool/service; eliminate model-supplied confirmation authority.
acceptance: A denied or absent approval produces zero business mutations.
Approving a different action or changed arguments fails; the successful operation returns factual state.
learning_outcomes: Separate user intent, human approval, and business authorization.
Understand the approval pause/resume lifecycle.
interview_questions: Why is a customerConfirmed argument supplied by the model insufficient?
What data must an approval be bound to?
tickets.stretch: Reject an action and verify the agent does not immediately repeat the same request.

tickets.title: Persist pending approvals and prevent duplicate operations
tickets.source_note: The course refund runner illustrates approval flow, not durable restart/resume or idempotency.
implementation: Persist conversation/pending-operation state and choose the appropriate checkpoint/session mechanism.
Use stable workflow/agent identities where required for restoration.
Add a durable operation key and state transition so an approved retry cannot refund twice.
acceptance: Restart between request and approval; resume the intended operation.
Duplicate approval/submission changes business state once; unknown or expired approval IDs are rejected.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish workflow durability from side-effect idempotency.
Understand restart/replay and stable identities.
interview_questions: Does checkpointing guarantee exactly-once external side effects?
What state must survive an approval wait and process restart?
tickets.stretch: Crash immediately after the fake refund commits and before the response is sent.

tickets.title: Implement streaming, cancellation, and terminal events
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Implement the shared event contract for progress, output, approval, error, and completion.
Propagate request cancellation through model/tool calls.
Choose buffered versus incremental filtering explicitly and measure time to first output.
acceptance: A successful stream has one terminal outcome and no hidden error after completion.
Client disconnect and tool failure stop or terminate predictably; partial structured output is not treated as a complete decision.
learning_outcomes: Understand asynchronous streaming and cancellation propagation.
Recognize filtering/latency tradeoffs.
interview_questions: How does transport streaming differ from actual model-token streaming?
How do you handle an error after an HTTP stream has begun?
tickets.stretch: Disconnect the client while a slow tool runs and inspect the trace.

tickets.title: Enforce customer access and conversation ownership
tickets.source_note: Course tools expose synthetic records without real access control; this ticket is an application-boundary extension.
implementation: Introduce a clearly documented local/test identity boundary.
Enforce order and conversation ownership in services using trusted request context.
Test cross-customer access and keep identity out of model-controlled authority.
acceptance: A customer cannot read another customer's order or resume their conversation.
An invented customer ID in tool arguments cannot override the authenticated/test principal.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish authentication, authorization, and model context.
Apply resource-level access controls to agent tools.
interview_questions: Where should authorization run in a tool-calling application?
Why does knowing an order ID not establish permission to access it?
tickets.stretch: Attempt cross-customer access through both the direct tool/service test and agent-facing API.

tickets.title: Validate tool boundaries and exercise prompt injection
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Validate tool argument types, ranges, allowlists, and output handling.
Exercise direct and tool-result injection using synthetic adversarial data.
Treat phrase filters as heuristics; enforce allowed actions before mutation.
acceptance: A malicious tool result cannot authorize a privileged operation.
False-positive/negative examples are documented; outputs are safely handled and traces contain no sensitive test payload by default.
learning_outcomes: Understand direct versus indirect prompt injection.
Separate detection heuristics from enforceable business controls.
interview_questions: Why are regex filters insufficient for prompt injection?
What happens when an LLM follows an instruction embedded in a tool result?
tickets.stretch: Create a paraphrased attack that bypasses the course phrase matcher and prove the operation gate still holds.

tickets.title: Add bounded timeouts, retries, and graceful failure
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Set explicit model/tool budgets and propagate cancellation.
Retry only eligible transient failures within a bound; protect writes using operation state.
Represent unavailable services and invalid model output without fabricated success.
acceptance: A deterministic fault fixture triggers the expected timeout/retry behavior.
Retries are bounded and visible; mutating operations are not duplicated; safe error responses retain a trace reference.
learning_outcomes: Classify transient failures versus invalid requests.
Understand resilience costs and retry amplification.
interview_questions: Which operations are safe to retry and why?
How can retries increase latency and model spend?
tickets.stretch: Combine a transient failure with cancellation and show the work stops.

tickets.title: Establish behavioral, latency, and usage baselines
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Run at least 20 shared scenarios covering success, ambiguity, invalid state, denial, and failures.
Report routing/tool/action outcomes and latency; collect provider-reported input/output usage.
Label cost estimates and unknown usage accurately; record model, versions, run count, and limitations.
acceptance: The evaluation produces a machine-readable result and a concise human report.
Offline deterministic checks and live-model evaluations are clearly separated; no exact-response-string equality is required.
learning_outcomes: Separate correctness evaluations from operational metrics.
Understand variability, sample size, and cost estimation.
interview_questions: How would you evaluate an agent beyond answer quality?
Why is self-reported model confidence not a substitute for labelled evaluation?
tickets.stretch: Change one prompt and compare behavior/cost with an unchanged evaluation set.

tickets.title: Scaffold Python packaging, health, and Aspire integration
tickets.source_note: The Python course setup is a reference for configuration; Aspire packaging and CI are extensions.
implementation: Create an idiomatic src/python package with pyproject.toml and uv.lock.
Implement configuration/health and add the process to the C# AppHost using the official integration.
Add import/lint/meaningful configuration checks to CI.
acceptance: Both backends start from AppHost and Python can also run independently.
A clean locked sync/import check passes without provider secrets; state directories remain separate.
learning_outcomes: Understand Python package/import structure and environment locking.
Compare hosting/configuration conventions across languages.
interview_questions: What is the role of uv.lock versus pyproject.toml?
How does Aspire launch a Python service while its logic stays independent?
tickets.stretch: Launch only Python outside Aspire using the documented configuration.

tickets.title: Implement Python agents, typed tools, and triage
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Implement the same three specialist domains with idiomatic Python typing and models.
Preserve original requests and validated fields through routing.
Reuse shared fixture/scenario contracts while keeping Python tool/service implementation independent.
acceptance: The same known/unknown record and routing checks pass against Python.
Invalid schema/category output reaches the controlled fallback.
learning_outcomes: Compare C# response types/executors with Python models/handlers.
Understand the common model/tool/workflow concepts.
interview_questions: Which differences are SDK conventions and which change observable behavior?
Where should Python validate model-generated values?
tickets.stretch: Implement an ambiguous routing scenario without consulting the C# code.

tickets.title: Implement Python sessions, approval persistence, and idempotency
tickets.source_note: The course always_require tools are useful; durable storage and business idempotency are added here.
implementation: Implement per-conversation sessions and framework-bound pending approvals.
Persist the required state and stable workflow identity.
Port the operation-level idempotency/authorization behavior through Python services.
acceptance: Approval denial, changed arguments, cross-conversation replay, and restart/resume cases pass.
Two repeated submissions produce one simulated business mutation.
learning_outcomes: Understand Python session-bound approval and durable state.
Separate language parity from line-by-line translation.
interview_questions: How does the current Python SDK bind an approval to a pending request?
Why should session state be isolated even when an agent definition is reusable?
tickets.stretch: Attempt a replay from a second conversation and inspect the rejection.

tickets.title: Implement Python streaming and correlated telemetry
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Implement the shared streaming/cancellation/error behavior.
Configure one telemetry setup with explicit service identity and exports.
Reconcile DevUI instrumentation with sensitive-data settings and avoid unintended duplicate providers/handlers.
acceptance: Python traces, logs, and metrics arrive in Aspire and meaningful events match the API contract.
Measure first-output latency and demonstrate whether middleware buffers; cancellation behaves as specified.
learning_outcomes: Understand async streams and middleware buffering.
Compare .NET and Python telemetry configuration and lifecycle ownership.
interview_questions: Why can a streamed API still buffer the entire answer?
How do provider setup and logger propagation cause duplicate telemetry?
tickets.stretch: Toggle the safe development telemetry setting and verify exactly what changes.

tickets.title: Run cross-language parity checks and document SDK decisions
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Run the same evaluation set against both backend endpoints with reset isolated state.
Classify differences as defect, intentional SDK difference, or model variability.
Write docs/decisions/0002-sdk-comparison.md covering tools, state, workflows, approvals, streaming, and diagnostics.
acceptance: Parity is assessed by routes, actions, schemas, and state outcomes.
Known differences and live-evaluation limits are explicit; deterministic regression checks join CI.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate behavioral equivalence without requiring identical prose.
Defend idiomatic implementation choices.
interview_questions: How do you prove two probabilistic implementations meet one specification?
What differences would influence your choice of SDK for a team?
tickets.stretch: Demonstrate a defect in one backend that the shared suite detects.

tickets.title: Finalize the frontend-facing protocol and stream/approval lifecycle
tickets.source_note: Chapter 7 hosting/approval behavior motivates the protocol; the course does not provide this frontend.
implementation: Validate the existing contracts against a minimal browser client and record protocol decisions.
Define session/backend binding, reconnect behavior, approval payloads, and terminal errors.
Add contract-level backend checks before implementing UI components.
acceptance: Example traces/messages cover chat, pending approval, rejection, timeout, and disconnection.
Backend selection is fixed per conversation and the browser never receives provider credentials.
learning_outcomes: Design a frontend around asynchronous workflow state.
Distinguish developer tools from a product interface.
interview_questions: What does the browser need to render a paused workflow?
How do you keep sessions coherent when two equivalent backends exist?
tickets.stretch: Specify how a refreshed browser discovers a pending approval.

tickets.title: Build shared chat UI with backend selection
tickets.source_note: Course composition roots are comparison references; this UI is original project work.
implementation: Choose and document a modest frontend stack; implement chat and new-conversation backend selection.
Render progress, streamed output, safe errors, and the current backend.
Register the frontend in AppHost with runtime endpoint configuration.
acceptance: One UI completes order-status conversations against either backend.
Backend selection cannot silently move an existing conversation; no provider key is shipped to the browser.
learning_outcomes: Consume a common API while keeping implementation choices behind it.
Understand frontend configuration and session identity.
interview_questions: Why choose the backend at conversation creation?
Which configuration is safe to expose to a browser?
tickets.stretch: Exercise the same prompt on both backends and compare results without changing UI code.

tickets.title: Add approval UI, recovery states, and trace references
tickets.source_note: Course approval tools teach the backend concept; browser state/recovery is an extension.
implementation: Display exact pending-action details with approve/reject controls.
Handle refresh, duplicate clicks, expired operations, and disconnected streams.
Display a support-safe trace reference for failures without exposing telemetry payloads.
acceptance: Rejecting an action results in zero mutation; duplicate approval cannot repeat it.
The UI recovers pending state and presents meaningful error/empty/loading states.
learning_outcomes: Turn workflow pause/resume into an understandable user interaction.
Understand server authority and resilient UI state.
interview_questions: Why must disabling an approval button not be the only duplicate-operation control?
What should the UI show when approval succeeds but the response connection fails?
tickets.stretch: Refresh immediately after approval submission and verify the final state.

tickets.title: Run fault, concurrency, and bounded load exercises
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Exercise concurrent conversations, slow providers, tool faults, restart/resume, and cancellations.
Measure bounded load with fake providers before any explicitly budgeted live run.
Record bottlenecks, resource limits, and one evidence-backed improvement.
acceptance: No cross-conversation leakage or duplicate mutation occurs in deterministic exercises.
A report states workload, sample counts, latency/error distributions, and limitations.
learning_outcomes: Understand throughput, backpressure, and state contention.
Use telemetry to diagnose rather than guess.
interview_questions: What fails first when traffic increases in this design?
How would you distinguish model latency from tool or application latency?
tickets.stretch: Demonstrate one regression and show the signal that reveals it.

tickets.title: Review dependencies, security checks, and operational limits
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Review dependency/secret protections and add appropriate language security/code-analysis checks for existing code.
Verify credential handling, access boundaries, sensitive telemetry policy, and data retention assumptions.
Update the threat model and list unresolved production requirements with owners/follow-up tasks.
acceptance: A documented review covers both backends and the browser surface.
CI/security checks run on the actual code; the repository does not claim production readiness without evidence.
learning_outcomes: Understand defense in depth and the limits of automation.
Communicate residual risk concretely.
interview_questions: What would you require before connecting this demo to real refunds or customer data?
Which controls are enforced by MAF and which belong to the application?
tickets.stretch: Trace one trust boundary from browser input to a mutating tool.

tickets.title: Publish the architecture, runbook, and portfolio demonstration
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Write a fresh-checkout runbook, architecture diagram, version table, and troubleshooting guide.
Prepare a short demonstration covering success, denial, a fault, and cross-language comparison.
Link sanitized evidence, decisions, and evaluation results; credit course inspiration.
acceptance: Another developer can follow the documented startup and verification steps.
The demonstration accurately separates implemented behavior, mock dependencies, and remaining work.
learning_outcomes: Explain a system clearly with evidence and limitations.
Turn implementation work into a defensible portfolio narrative.
interview_questions: Walk me through an end-to-end request and its failure path.
What did you change from the course and why?
tickets.stretch: Ask someone to follow the runbook without verbal guidance and record the gaps.

tickets.title: Complete a mock interview and independent change exercise
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Answer the accumulated ticket questions in your own words using the evidence notes.
Demonstrate diagnosis of an injected fault from traces/metrics/logs.
Implement a small new requirement independently, then review its design and tests.
acceptance: Document answers, weak areas, and follow-up practice honestly.
Explain SDK selection, workflows, approvals, state, telemetry, evaluation, and deployment gaps without reading generated answers.
learning_outcomes: Synthesize implementation knowledge and engineering judgment.
Communicate tradeoffs under interview-style constraints.
interview_questions: Why did you choose this architecture, and when would you simplify it?
What would you change for a production service handling real customer actions?
tickets.stretch: Add a read-only return-eligibility query and justify its tool, policy, evaluation, and observability design.
